answers.justification: C5 shows Pellacott-2026 claim rates are the same for legacy and new installers (41 vs 42), Durrant-Hale units run at 5–7 in every installer group, brazed joints are intact and never-installed Pellacott 2026 valves leak (11%). E5/C6 are confounded by build year (new firms install mostly 2026-built units), and C1 shows clean onboarding.

C10 found rig LT-04 out of service since 9 Jan 2026, no VA-220 program on any other rig, no backup rig, and per-piece tables recycled from four Nov-2025 sequences. C5 shows 2026 Pellacott valves are defective (11% seat leakage when never installed vs 1/100 for 2025-built and 0/100 for Durrant-Hale).

The valves are defective (C5), but C10 shows the recorded LT-04 tests could not have been performed: the rig failed in Jan 2026 and the certificate values are copied sequences. That contradicts the 'tests actually performed' part of H3.

C5 shows Pellacott-2026 claim rates are about the same on firmware 4.1 (40) and 4.2 (42), and Durrant-Hale units stay at 5–7 in every firmware group. The rise also starts with January builds, before the 10 Mar rollout (E2, C2).

C8 shows programme-wide test-record conformance jumped (71 to 96) and SupplierPath never collects rig logs, so other suppliers could be doing the same. However, no evidence directly shows fabrication by any supplier other than Pellacott.

Temporal onset with 2026 Pellacott builds (E2, E4), a seal-deformation mechanism (C5 teardown), a bench defect in never-installed valves, and a within-stratum supplier contrast (about 41 vs 5–7 across all installer and firmware groups) together rule out the main rivals (C5).

With valve source held fixed, claim rates do not differ between new and legacy installers (C5 item 3). The apparent installer pattern in E5/C6 is explained by new firms installing mostly 2026-built units.
C5 shows no difference between 4.1 and 4.2 units within each valve source, C2 lab validation found no valve faults, and claims were already high for Jan–Feb builds, before the update.

Deformed slide seals co-occur with the Corlin switch (C5, C11: compression set never tested on production lots), but every 2026 sample also has Line 3 assembly, so the seal source cannot be separated from the line move (C5 item 4).

By the scoring formula in E3, test-record conformance rising from 58 to 100 adds about 17 points. Without it, Pellacott's Q3 score would be about 72, below the 85 dock-to-stock threshold, while the audit component barely moved (74 to 79; C3, E3).

Never-installed 2026 Pellacott stock leaks at 11% under helium (C5) and its certificates are unreliable (C10), so quarantining, suspending dock-to-stock and verifying with Brenmoor's own testing is the protective step. Durrant-Hale supply (C9) gives a route to reduce the line stoppage.
C5 shows installers are not the cause, so suspending the new firms and charging claims back to them would punish the wrong party.

Fresh Pellacott certificates are worthless because the rig they cite has been out of service since January and the values are recycled (C10). Releasing the lots would ship valves from a population with an 11% seat-leak rate (C5).
The seal switch and the Line 3 move are confounded (C5 item 4) and the seal compound has not been analysed, so committing to Ferrand as the fix is not yet justified.

C8 and C13 show SupplierPath awards credit for unverified paperwork and grants dock-to-stock automatically, and C10 shows that gap was exploited. Requiring rig logs or witnessed tests closes the control gap, though waiting for the next audit cycle is slow given that 15 suppliers are on dock-to-stock.

The independent rig observation (C10) plus the warehouse helium retest and stratified claims (C5) are enough to commit to A1's quarantine and suspension now, even though the precise root cause (seal vs line) is unresolved.

ambiguousItems: I15: preferred vs acceptable. It is a sound systemic fix, but 'starting from the next audit cycle' delays action while 15 suppliers sit on dock-to-stock under the same unverified-paperwork rule, and the immediate priority is A1.
I5: unknown vs weakly supported. The programme-wide conformance jump with no rig-log collection (C8) is suggestive but not direct evidence of fabrication by other suppliers.
I9: association-only vs unknown. The seal mechanism is plausible, but the full confound with Line 3 might lead some to call it unknown.
caseProblems: C10 is close to decisive by itself (rig dead since Jan, no other VA-220 program, copied value sequences), so H2 vs H3 hinges almost entirely on one item.

C5 item 3 does a clean stratification of claims by supplier, installer and firmware, even though E2 says the dashboard cannot split claims by source, installer or firmware. The case should state how the lab obtained that split (e.g., serial-number matching).

C3 records LT-04 calibration certificates 'all in date' at the 30 Sep audit, although C10 shows the rig failed on 9 Jan. This is consistent with fraud but is not flagged, and solvers may read it as an inconsistency.
Minor: E2's Jan 2026 build month already shows 22 claims per 1,000, which needs most January builds to contain post-12-Jan Pellacott valves. That is plausible but implicit.

rulings.explanation: The scoring flaw is well established. E3 and C8 show credit for unverified, self-reported records with automatic dock-to-stock, C13 shows no rig logs were asked for, and C10 shows the records were fabricated. A5 is the direct systemic fix. Of the five actions, A2 and A3 are harmful and A4 is premature, so A5 is clearly the second-best option. That makes 'among the best next actions' a reasonable reading. The key's case for 'acceptable' depends on 'starting from the next audit cycle' being a costly delay. But scores are only computed each quarter, so the next cycle is the earliest point a scoring rule can take effect, and the wording is not clearly a defect. The key's other concern, the 15 existing dock-to-stock grants, appears only in the rationale. A5's text does not say those grants stay in place, so a careful analyst can reasonably read A5 as a preferred companion to A1. The blind expert did exactly that and still noted the delay. Both 'preferred' and 'acceptable' are defensible.
rulings.fix: Make the gap explicit in A5's wording, for example: 'Change SupplierPath scoring so that submitted test records earn credit only when backed by rig logs or a witnessed test, starting from the next audit cycle; existing dock-to-stock grants remain in place until each supplier's next scheduled score.' Optionally add to C8 that the next scoring cycle closes in late December 2026. 'Acceptable' then becomes the only defensible answer: the action is sound but leaves the 15 unverified grants in place in the meantime.

rulings.explanation: 'Weakly supported' is not an allowed answer, so the real choice is between 'supported' and 'unknown'. C8 and E3 show conformance rising across the programme (71 to 96; 19 of 22 suppliers at 95 or above) and that rig logs are never collected. That shows opportunity and incentive. It does not tell fabrication apart from the obvious rival: suppliers legitimately completing their paperwork once the score rewarded it. Pellacott's own 2025 shortfall was missing values, not failing ones. The modest rise in the audit component and Tanvik's larger gain fit both explanations. No catalogue item checks another supplier's rig logs or raw data. The claim is live but not established, so 'unknown' is the only defensible answer. 'Supported' would treat a lack of verification as evidence of fabrication.

Under the case's definitions, 'unknown' means the evidence is not enough even to show association. Here association is clearly shown. Every 2026-built Pellacott valve has the Corlin seal. C5 finds 11% seat leakage in never-installed 2026 stock against 1 in 100 for 2025-built (Ferrand) stock, and teardowns place the defect in the slide seal itself. C5 also says outright that the seal compound was not analysed and that the Corlin seal and Line 3 are fully confounded, so 'causal' is ruled out. C11's untested compression-set data adds plausibility but does not separate the two. The confound blocks a causal finding; it does not cancel the association. 'Association-only' is the only defensible answer.
